about: External reference values for the clinician view (D2). There are no published norms for network-level metrics, so every entry is a norm for the behaviour a network metric stands in for (sleep timing and duration, screen time, night-time phone use, sleep regularity) and carries a proxy_note. Every value was checked in the full text of its source on 2026-11-20 (location gives table/page). Units are those of the portal tracks: clock times as minutes from midnight (negative = evening before), durations in hours (quiet_hours, online_hours) or minutes (night_minutes, quiet_start_sd7). stat says what a value is: mean_sd (mean and SD of individuals), mean_sd_by_age (one mean/SD row per year of age), median, mean, pooled_mean (meta-analytic pooled mean of study means: centre only, no spread of individuals).

maslowsky2014.citation: Maslowsky J, Ozer EJ. Developmental trends in sleep duration in adolescence and young adulthood: evidence from a national United States sample. J Adolesc Health. 2014;54(6):691-697. doi:10.1016/j.jadohealth.2013.10.201
maslowsky2014.population: US National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health), waves 1-4 (1994-2008), N = 15,701 people, 52,080 observations, ages 13-32
maslowsky2014.method: self-report: waves 1-2 'How many hours of sleep do you usually get?' (whole hours); waves 3-4 usual bed and wake times on work/school days and free days, weighted 5/7 and 2/7

galland2018.citation: Galland BC, Short MA, Terrill P, et al. Establishing normal values for pediatric nighttime sleep measured by actigraphy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep. 2018;41(4):zsy017. doi:10.1093/sleep/zsy017
galland2018.population: meta-analysis of actigraphy studies, ages 3-18; 15-18 y band: 3-9 datasets per variable
galland2018.method: actigraphy; pooled mean estimates (95% CI) of study means. Sleep duration = sleep onset to offset (excludes latency); weekend/nonschool = weekend days in all but one dataset

james2024.citation: Külling-Knecht C, Waller G, Willemse I, et al. JAMES - Jugend, Aktivitäten, Medien - Erhebung Schweiz. Zürich: ZHAW; 2024
james2024.population: Swiss 12-19-year-olds, all three language regions, net sample N = 1,183 (§2.2, p. 5)
james2024.method: self-report questionnaire in school classes: internet use on a typical weekday and a weekend day

alexander2024.citation: Alexander JD, Linkersdörfer J, Toda-Thorne K, et al. Passively sensing smartphone use in teens with rates of use by sex and across operating systems. Sci Rep. 2024;14:17982. doi:10.1038/s41598-024-68467-8
alexander2024.population: US ABCD study, youth with passively sensed app use (about 475; t-test df = 474), age about 14 (Android users: M 14.0, SD 0.70, range 12.6-15.8, Table 2)
alexander2024.method: EARS app, three weeks of passively logged smartphone app use; no significant weekday/weekend difference

jonasdottir2021.citation: Jonasdottir SS, Minor K, Lehmann S. Gender differences in nighttime sleep patterns and variability across the adult lifespan: a global-scale wearables study. Sleep. 2021;44(2):zsaa169. doi:10.1093/sleep/zsaa169
jonasdottir2021.population: 69,650 adult non-shift workers aged 19-67 from 47 countries, 11.14 million nights (abstract)
jonasdottir2021.method: consumer wristband; intra-individual variability = SD of a person's sleep onset times, computed separately for weekdays and weekends (Methods, p. 3)

mathew2026.citation: Mathew G, Rodriguez I, Reichenberger D, Christakis D, Hale L. Pre-bedtime smartphone use predicts higher within-person likelihood of late-night smartphone use among adolescents: the SBU MEDiA study. Sleep. 2026;49(Suppl 1):A106-A107, abstract 0242. doi:10.1093/sleep/zsag091.0242
mathew2026.population: US adolescents owning a smartphone, n = 229 (age not reported in the abstract); conference abstract, not a full paper
mathew2026.method: RealityMeter, passively measured smartphone use over 16.8 ± 13.7 days

windred2024.citation: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al. Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: a prospective cohort study. Sleep. 2024;47(1):zsad253. doi:10.1093/sleep/zsad253
windred2024.population: UK Biobank, 60,977 adults, age 62.8 ± 7.8 years, 55.0% female (abstract)
windred2024.method: wrist accelerometer for 7 days; Sleep Regularity Index (SRI, 0-100)

entries.location: Table 1 (mean sleep duration M (SD) by age)
entries.label: self-reported sleep, Add Health
entries.proxy_note: Self-reported usual sleep (US, 1994-2008, mostly before smartphones), weighted over the week. The quiet window is only an upper bound for the time asleep: asleep, away and devices switched off look the same, and a phone used in bed shortens it.

entries.location: Table 4, p. 9 (all days); Table 5, p. 10 (weekday vs weekend/nonschool)
entries.label: sleep duration 15-18 y, actigraphy
entries.proxy_note: Actigraphy sleep duration (sleep onset to offset). The quiet window starts when the last device goes quiet, not at sleep onset, and also covers away and switched-off nights. Pooled mean of study means: the centre only, not the spread between people.

entries.label: sleep onset 15-18 y, actigraphy
entries.proxy_note: Actigraphy sleep onset. 'Went quiet' is when the devices stop being in use: phone use in bed makes it later than lights-out, and a device left on (or a quiet phone in bed) separates it from falling asleep. Pooled mean of study means, no spread between people.

entries.label: sleep offset 15-18 y, actigraphy
entries.proxy_note: Actigraphy sleep offset (waking up). 'Back online' is the first use of a device after the night: someone can be awake for a while before touching a device. Pooled mean of study means, no spread between people.

entries.location: §7.1, Table 3, p. 37 (median 3 h 7 min weekday, 4 h 30 min weekend day; mean 3 h 41 min, 5 h 12 min)
entries.label: online time 12-19 y, self-report (CH)
entries.proxy_note: Self-reported time online on any network. Time in use counts 5-minute bins with traffic on the home Wi-Fi only: background traffic of a device in use, shared devices and use at home all differ from 'online time', and mobile data is not seen.

entries.location: Results, 'Descriptives of youth who participated in passive sensing' (298 ± 174 min/day app use; self-report 185 ± 162 min); Table 2 (age)
entries.label: smartphone use 12-15 y, passively logged
entries.proxy_note: Passively logged smartphone app use (US, about 14 years old). Time in use counts home Wi-Fi traffic of all the person's devices, so it can be higher (laptop, background traffic) or lower (mobile data) than phone screen time. The distribution is right-skewed, so a normal range from mean ± SD is rough.

entries.age_note: adolescents; age not reported in the abstract
entries.location: abstract 0242, Methods: late-night use 0:00-5:00 on school nights, 1:00-6:00 on non-school nights, M = 46.74 min
entries.label: late-night phone use, adolescents
entries.proxy_note: Passively logged smartphone use in a late-night window (00-05 on school nights, 01-06 otherwise). Use at night counts home Wi-Fi traffic between 00:00 and 06:00 on all devices; mobile data is not seen. Conference abstract: mean only.

entries.location: Results, 'Sleep variability over the lifespan', p. 10 and Figure 7 (onset variability nearly fixed across the lifespan at 1.1 h on weekdays and 1.3 h on weekends)
entries.label: sleep-onset variability, adults, wearables
entries.proxy_note: Average within-person SD of sleep onset over the whole recording, separately for weekdays and weekends (adults 19-67). Ours is the SD of the went-quiet time over the last 7 nights, weekdays and weekends together, so it is not directly comparable; 'went quiet' is not sleep onset.

entries.label: Sleep Regularity Index, UK Biobank adults
entries.proxy_note: Context only, not used for a range: the SRI compares sleep/wake state 24 h apart in older adults; our irregular-nights measure is the SD of the went-quiet time and has no SRI equivalent.
